advanced.input.description: These settings control where the input is read from, whether the program tries to automatically find a Morsewurst device on serial ports, and whether an incomplete round is finished after a long pause.
advanced.input.use_telemetry_as_truth_hi: Recommendation: keep enabled. The round is scored from raw telemetry (actual key press timings). If disabled, the program uses USB HID keyboard input, which is not accurate enough for reliable scoring.
advanced.input.auto_connect_serial: Try to connect to serial port automatically
advanced.input.keyboard_description: With this setting, the computer keyboard acts as a virtual straight key. Key presses generate the same raw telemetry as a physical Morsewurst device.
advanced.input.keyboard_note: When enabled, the program uses the selected key as a virtual straight key, forces telemetry as truth, and disables automatic serial port scanning. Note that the keyboard is not a reliable or accurate Morse key.
advanced.input.auto_finish_description: This finishes the round if telemetry has arrived but the input remains too short, for example due to missing character gaps.

advanced.adaptive.title: Decoder & timing profile

advanced.sound.title: Sounds

advanced.stats.title: General information history

help.content.title: Morsewurst help
help.content.intro: Morsewurst is a desktop application for practising Morse code with real timing data. It is built around the idea that Morse practice should not only compare typed characters, but also understand rhythm, timing, gaps, speed, accuracy and long term progress. The program works best with the homemade ESP32-S3 based Morsewurst Keyer, because that device sends very accurate raw timing telemetry from the key itself. The hardware project and application source are available at https://github.com/kasperikoski/morsewurst. Building the keyer is warmly recommended, because it makes Morsewurst much more than a normal typing trainer and turns it into a practical and enjoyable hardware project.
help.content.prototype_note: Morsewurst is still actively developed. The main practice features, local history, skill calculation and network functions are usable, but some details may change between releases. The Reddit community at https://www.reddit.com/r/Morsewurst/ is a good place to ask for help, discuss the program, report bugs and suggest improvements.
help.content.getting_started.heading: Getting started
help.content.getting_started.intro: A typical session starts by choosing or creating a user profile, connecting an input source, selecting what to practise and starting a practice series. Morsewurst then generates target text, listens to your Morse, decodes the telemetry, saves each finished round and updates the result, history and skill panels.
help.content.getting_started.profile: On the first launch Morsewurst checks the application data folder for existing profiles. If no profile exists, the program asks you to create one before normal use. Profiles keep practice history, settings, network settings and debug files separate, so the same computer can be used by more than one person without mixing results.
help.content.getting_started.device: For the most accurate experience, use the Morsewurst Keyer or another compatible device that sends raw serial telemetry. The telemetry contains exact press and release times, source information such as straight or iambic, and element hints when the firmware provides them. This is much more useful for scoring than ordinary keyboard text.
help.content.getting_started.settings: The Practice settings panel controls the next practice series. You can choose letters, numbers and punctuation, set the number of groups, choose the character range inside each group, set the target WPM, enable WX-MOR weather style messages, practise difficult characters and ask Morsewurst to suggest a practice speed from your history.
help.content.getting_started.start: You can start a practice series from the Start practice button. When the program is idle, you can also press the key seven times within about three seconds. Morsewurst then shows a short countdown bar and starts the practice automatically. This is useful when your hands are already on the key.
help.content.getting_started.results: After each completed round, Morsewurst saves the round and updates the Result panel, Latest round, General information, Skill level, Most difficult characters, Recent rounds and Statistics window. A practice series is also tracked as a whole, so the program knows whether the series completed, stopped or was interrupted.
help.content.input.heading: Input modes and connection
help.content.input.intro: Morsewurst can read Morse from raw telemetry, USB HID text and a virtual keyboard Morse mode. Raw telemetry is the recommended mode because it gives the decoder and scoring system the real timing data.
help.content.input.telemetry: Use telemetry as truth means that the saved answer is based on decoded raw timing events instead of ordinary text typed by the operating system. This is the preferred setting for accurate scoring, adaptive decoding, timing analysis, raw telemetry drawing, skill calculation and problem character tracking.
help.content.input.hid: USB HID text can be useful as a fallback because the device can type decoded characters into the input field. It is not as good for scoring, because the operating system receives characters rather than the original press and gap timings. HID text can show what the device thought you sent, but it cannot replace telemetry for rhythm analysis.
help.content.input.keyboard: Keyboard Morse lets one computer keyboard key act as a virtual straight key. You can choose keys such as Space, Enter, arrow keys, Ctrl, Shift, Alt or function keys. This is convenient for testing, but a normal keyboard has latency and key repeat behaviour that make it less reliable than a real Morse key.
help.content.input.autoconnect: Automatic serial connection scans serial ports and looks for the expected Morsewurst device heartbeat. When a compatible device is found, Morsewurst connects to it automatically and begins reading telemetry. If a port is busy, another program or the automatic scanner may already be using it.
help.content.input.note: When Keyboard Morse is enabled, Morsewurst forces telemetry as truth and disables automatic serial port scanning. This prevents the virtual keyboard key from fighting with a physical device and keeps the input source clear.
help.content.practice_settings.heading: Practice settings
help.content.practice_settings.intro: The Practice settings panel is the main place for choosing what the next practice will contain. It affects the generated target, the reference timing, the number of rounds and whether special modes such as WX-MOR or difficult character practice are used.
help.content.practice_settings.character: Letters A-Z, numbers 0-9 and punctuation can be enabled separately and combined freely. You can practise only letters, only numbers, only punctuation or any mixture of them. If all groups are turned off, Morsewurst uses letters and numbers as a safe fallback so the generated target is never empty.

The Character mix bar controls the long-term target balance between the enabled groups. With two enabled groups there is one draggable boundary, with three enabled groups there are two boundaries, and with one enabled group the whole bar belongs to that group. Disabled groups are ignored by the generator, but their last saved values can remain in settings for later use.

The mix is probabilistic, not a promise that every short round contains every selected group. For example, a 1 percent punctuation share means each generated character has a small chance to come from punctuation, so many short rounds may contain none.
help.content.practice_settings.groups: Groups min and Groups max control how many groups of characters are generated. Chars min and Chars max control how many characters appear inside each group. These settings make it possible to practise short fragments, longer groups or more realistic message like targets.
help.content.practice_settings.wpm: Target WPM is the reference speed for the current challenge. It affects the reference time, speed score, audio test and several timing expectations. The adaptive decoder still learns from your actual rhythm, so the target WPM is a starting point and scoring reference rather than a hard decoding lock.
help.content.practice_settings.rounds: Rounds defines how many individual rounds belong to one practice series. Each finished round is saved separately, and the whole series is also tracked as one practice. This helps Morsewurst handle normal completion, stopping and interruption more intelligently.
help.content.practice_settings.wxmor: WX-MOR is a compact weather message format created by the developer of this program for Morse practice. It is inspired by aviation weather messages such as METAR, but it is its own Morse training format. More information is available at https://kasperikoski.fi/wx.
help.content.practice_settings.problem_c: Practice most difficult characters adds extra weight to characters that have caused the most errors in recent history. It does not replace the selected character set or override the character mix. Morsewurst first chooses a group from the character mix, then applies difficult-character weighting only inside that chosen group.

The difficult-character percentage is also a long-term weighting. If letters are chosen for a character position, the difficult-letter list can be used according to the configured weight. If numbers are chosen, only difficult numbers are considered. If punctuation is chosen, only difficult punctuation is considered. When a selected group has no matching difficult characters yet, Morsewurst falls back to normal random selection inside that group.
help.content.practice_settings.suggest_s: Suggest practice speed uses recent accurate and clean saved rounds to estimate a reasonable target WPM. The calculation is based on actual PARIS speed from round duration and target Morse units, and it uses the limits chosen in the Effective WPM settings.
help.content.koch.heading: Koch receive practice
help.content.koch.intro: The Koch button opens a separate receive-practice window. Koch practice plays a generated target and hides the target text until scoring, so the exercise is focused on copying what you hear.
help.content.koch.modes: Guided mode opens characters step by step. Manual stage lets you choose the stage directly. Full charset uses the whole supported Morsewurst character set without guided progression.
help.content.koch.sequence_stage: Sequence chooses Classic Koch or LCWO. Progress, current stage and the five-failure counter are tracked separately for each order, so training one order does not overwrite the other.
help.content.koch.speed_audio: Character WPM controls the speed of the dots, dashes and intra-character gaps inside each Morse character. Farnsworth WPM controls the overall copy speed by lengthening only the gaps between characters and words or groups. The normal 3-unit character gap and 7-unit word/group gap relationship is preserved. Tone Hz and Volume % affect only the local playback sound.
help.content.koch.target_length: Target chars controls the generated copy length. Very short drills are automatically raised to a useful minimum so that the active characters, especially the newest character, can appear often enough.
help.content.koch.scoring: A guided stage is passed only when copy accuracy, cleanliness and the new-character checks reach the configured targets. The result view also shows timing accuracy, timing fit, errors and whether the session passed.
help.content.koch.guided_progress: If five consecutive pass-eligible guided sessions on the same sequence and stage stay below the target, the current stage is lowered by one. The unlocked stage is not reduced, and the counter is stored in the profile database.
help.content.koch.skill: Koch copy skill appears after at least 30 Koch sessions. It uses recent Koch sessions, currently up to 1000, and combines current character coverage, average accuracy, cleanliness, character WPM, Farnsworth WPM and target length.
help.content.koch.radio_noise: Koch playback can include quiet generated radio-style background noise. The noise is local ambience mixed into the generated exercise audio, with fade and filtering, and is meant to make receiving feel alive without masking the Morse tone.
help.content.koch.note: Koch receive skill is separate from the normal sending skill rating. Normal Morse practice scoring is not changed by Koch settings.
help.content.round.heading: The practice round
help.content.round.intro: A round begins when Morsewurst shows a target and starts accepting input. The clock starts from the first real input event, not merely from the moment the target appears. This makes timing fairer when you need a moment before sending.
help.content.round.target: The Target field shows the text you are supposed to send. In normal practice this is generated from the selected letters, numbers, punctuation, character mix, group limits and WPM settings. In WX-MOR mode it contains a compact weather style message.
help.content.round.raw: Raw telemetry shows the actual keying pattern received from the device. It is a visual timing display of elements and gaps. It helps you see whether dots, dashes, intra-character gaps, letter gaps and word gaps are behaving as expected.
help.content.round.decoded: Decoded from telemetry shows the text that Morsewurst decoded from the raw timing events. When telemetry as truth is enabled, this is the input used for scoring the round. It can differ from HID text if the firmware or operating system produced different characters.
help.content.round.clock: The timer compares your elapsed time with the reference time estimated from the target text and target WPM. The reference is based on Morse timing rather than just character count, so long punctuation or spaces can affect the expected time.
help.content.round.finish: A round finishes when the decoded telemetry or input matches the expected target sufficiently for completion, or when the automatic idle finish detects a long pause after received telemetry. By default the automatic finish waits for at least 14 timing units and at least 2 seconds, and both values can be changed in settings.
help.content.round.stop: Stop practice cancels a countdown or stops the current series. An unfinished active round is discarded rather than saved, while rounds that were already saved remain in the database. If the application is closed during a practice series, the practice can be marked as interrupted so the database does not pretend it completed normally.
help.content.round.auto_finish_note: Automatic finish after silence is meant for situations where some telemetry arrived but the round cannot complete normally, for example because a final character gap never arrives. The required idle time is calculated from the current timing unit and the user setting, but it is never shorter than the configured minimum seconds.
help.content.scoring.heading: Result panel and scoring
help.content.scoring.intro: The Result panel summarizes the current practice series and the latest saved round. It separates accuracy, cleanliness, timing, speed and WPM values so that you can see whether problems come from wrong characters, extra or missing characters, rhythm or speed.
help.content.scoring.accuracy: Accuracy describes how well the entered text matches the target text. It focuses on correct characters and edit distance. Substitutions, insertions and deletions reduce the result.
help.content.scoring.cleanliness: Cleanliness describes how cleanly the target was sent without extra noise, missing material or unnecessary edits. It is useful because a round can contain many correct characters and still be messy.
help.content.scoring.overall: The overall score combines the main learning metrics. The current weighting is 60 percent accuracy, 20 percent cleanliness, 10 percent speed and 10 percent timing. This makes correctness most important, but still rewards rhythm and appropriate speed.
help.content.scoring.timing: Timing measures Morse rhythm. For straight key use, Morsewurst can evaluate dot consistency, dash consistency, dash to dot ratio, intra-character gaps, letter gaps and word gaps. For iambic keyer use, the keyer creates the elements, so the program focuses mainly on the manual letter and word gaps.
help.content.scoring.paris: PARIS WPM is the actual demonstrated speed calculated from the Morse units in the target and the round duration. It is often a better speed measure than a plain character count because Morse characters have different lengths.
help.content.scoring.net: Net WPM is a practical speed value that can be adjusted by timing quality. It tries to describe useful, understandable Morse speed rather than merely how quickly something was sent.
help.content.scoring.device: Device WPM is the speed reported or implied by the device telemetry when available. It can be useful for comparison, but Morsewurst primarily relies on saved round data and PARIS timing for training statistics.
help.content.scoring.ratio: Dash to dot ratio shows how close straight key dashes are to the expected three dot length. A ratio near 3.0 is the usual Morse rhythm target. This value is most meaningful for straight key use.
help.content.scoring.formula:
Overall score = accuracy * 0.60 + cleanliness * 0.20 + speed * 0.10 + timing * 0.10
Letter gap target = about 3 units
Word gap target = about 7 units
Straight key dash target = about 3 dots
help.content.scoring.spaces_note: Spaces matter because word gaps are part of Morse. A missing or extra space can change both the decoded text and the timing analysis.
help.content.decoder.heading: Decoder and timing profile
help.content.decoder.intro: The adaptive decoder turns raw tone events into characters. It starts from the target WPM, the device telemetry and the selected settings, then learns practical timing from recent good rounds when timing profiles are enabled.
help.content.decoder.target_seed: Target WPM gives the decoder an initial estimate of one timing unit. In standard Morse timing, one PARIS unit can be estimated from 1,200,000 divided by WPM in microseconds. This estimate helps at the beginning of a round.
help.content.decoder.profile: The learned timing profile stores separate rhythm estimates for straight and iambic use. It is built from recent good rounds. By default it needs enough evidence before it is trusted, and the progress bar in the Decoder tab shows whether the profile is still gathering data, almost ready or active.
help.content.decoder.sources: Straight and iambic are treated differently. With a straight key, the user controls dot length, dash length and all gaps. With an iambic keyer, the firmware controls elements and intra-character spacing, so Morsewurst relies more on telemetry element units and evaluates the manual gaps between letters and words.
help.content.decoder.confidence: Profile confidence grows as more suitable rounds are collected and as timing stays stable. The default goal for a fully confident profile is much higher than a few rounds, because one or two good rounds should not permanently redefine your rhythm.
help.content.decoder.profile_quality: For timing profile learning, Morsewurst prefers rounds with enough target characters, high accuracy, high cleanliness and acceptable timing. The important default thresholds are at least 12 target characters, at least 90 percent accuracy, at least 85 percent cleanliness and at least 30 percent timing score for profile eligibility.
help.content.decoder.raw_truth: Use telemetry as truth should normally stay enabled. It lets the decoder and scoring system work from actual key press and release timings. If it is disabled, Morsewurst can fall back to text input, but detailed rhythm analysis becomes much weaker.
help.content.decoder.units:
One timing unit is the basic dot length.
Intra-character gap target is about 1 unit.
Letter gap target is about 3 units.
Word gap target is about 7 units.
Iambic telemetry can provide a real element unit, and Morsewurst can use that measured unit instead of relying only on target WPM.
help.content.decoder.note: The raw telemetry display can be scaled with Pixels per timing unit. This only changes the visual display. It does not change the saved telemetry or the score.
help.content.skill.heading: Skill level
help.content.skill.intro: The Skill level panel estimates practical Morse ability from saved history. It is designed to describe how well the user can send understandable, accurate and rhythmic Morse, not just how fast the fastest round was.
help.content.skill.overall: Overall skill WPM is the most realistic single skill value. It uses recent sufficiently long rounds, quality factors, character mastery, coverage and timing stability. Poor rounds are not simply ignored, because they are evidence about practical sending ability.
help.content.skill.both_keys: Both keys WPM is based on suitable straight and iambic evidence together. The model balances both key sources, and confidence is limited by the weaker side. Straight WPM and Iambic WPM shown in the panel are displayed as uncapped PARIS speeds from qualified rounds when available, while the internal model can still use capped evidence to avoid over-crediting a round practised at a low target WPM.
help.content.skill.level: The level title is derived from the raw skill value. Possible titles include No level yet, First steps, Beginner, Trainee, Basic level, Developing operator, Skilled operator, Advanced operator, Experienced operator, Fast operator and Elite operator.
help.content.skill.confidence: Confidence combines sample size, character mastery and coverage. If the estimate is preliminary, the panel can still show a level, but it warns that more data is needed. A reliable estimate currently expects at least 50 qualified rounds from the weaker key source.
help.content.skill.mastery: Character mastery looks at attempts, correct characters, errors and whether the expected character set has been covered enough. A character generally needs several attempts before the model treats it as properly covered.
help.content.skill.not_enough: A round must have at least 12 target characters excluding spaces before it can be used for skill rating. Qualified WPM evidence also requires at least 90 percent accuracy and 85 percent cleanliness. Timing quality is calculated from the same kind of good, long rounds when enough telemetry exists.
help.content.history.heading: History and saved data
help.content.history.intro: Morsewurst saves finished rounds into the local profile database. Each saved round contains the target, entered or decoded text, score summary, timing values, telemetry events and character level results when available. Practice series are also tracked separately from individual rounds.
help.content.history.recent: Recent rounds shows saved rounds in a table with ID, time, accuracy, cleanliness, score, errors, PARIS WPM, duration, input and target. Opening a history round lets you inspect an older result without changing the active practice.
help.content.history.general: General information on the main page shows historical averages from the latest saved rounds. The number of recent rounds used for these averages is controlled in the General information tab of Settings. The calculation uses the latest saved rounds up to that amount, regardless of round quality.
help.content.history.stats: Statistics opens a larger window with date range controls, quick ranges for 30 days, 90 days, one year and all data, a bucket selector and charts. The available buckets are Auto, Raw, 15 min, 1 hour, Day, Week and Month. Raw shows individual saved values. The time buckets group values and show the average inside each bucket. The chart tabs show WPM, Quality, Skill and Problem characters.
help.content.history.delete: Delete sessions opens the Poista harjoituksia or Delete practice sessions window. It can refresh the list, count a selected time range, delete one selected session, delete all sessions in a time range or delete all sessions. Deletion removes the session and related telemetry, character results and skill snapshots, and it cannot be undone.
help.content.advanced.heading: Settings tabs
help.content.advanced.intro: The Settings window contains the detailed configuration tabs used by Morsewurst. Most users can keep the defaults, but the tabs make it possible to adjust language, speed, decoder learning, difficult character weighting, sounds, input behaviour, effective WPM, skill level history, general information and debug data.
help.content.advanced.speed: Speed contains Target WPM, Audio test and Suggest practice speed. Target WPM is the reference speed for the next challenge. Audio test previews the Morse speed. Suggest practice speed reads recent suitable history and proposes a target that is challenging but still realistic.
help.content.advanced.input: Input and connection contains Use telemetry as truth, Keep input field active, automatic serial connection, Keyboard Morse and Automatic finish after long pause. The automatic finish defaults to 14 silence units and a minimum of 2 seconds, and the user can change both values.
help.content.advanced.decoder: Decoder contains the learned rhythm profile, separate Straight and Iambic summaries, profile confidence, profile progress, learning settings, automatic round finish and Raw telemetry display scaling. Use learned timing profile lets Morsewurst seed the decoder from your recent rhythm instead of relying only on target WPM.
help.content.advanced.problem_chars: Problem characters controls how strongly difficult characters are weighted, how many problem characters can be used and how many recent rounds are examined. It is meant to guide practice toward weak spots without turning the whole session into only error characters.
help.content.advanced.sound: Sounds contains the master Sounds enabled switch and individual event sounds. Current event sounds include practice series complete, serial device connected, serial device disconnected and level up. The level-up sound is used only when a newly saved practice update raises the visible level, not when old history is merely loaded.
help.content.advanced.koch: Koch contains scoring behaviour for Koch receive practice, including the automatic scoring delay after playback. The main Koch window contains the everyday controls for mode, order, stage, Character WPM, Farnsworth WPM, tone, volume and length.
help.content.advanced.effective: Effective WPM controls how Morsewurst estimates a suggested practice speed. It uses recent rounds that pass the selected minimum accuracy and cleanliness thresholds, then calculates actual PARIS WPM from target Morse units and round duration.
help.content.advanced.skill: Skill level controls how many recent rounds are considered by the skill rating calculation. The model uses sufficiently long rounds and combines effective WPM, accuracy, cleanliness, character mastery, coverage and timing. A longer history gives the estimate more stability.
help.content.advanced.stats: General information controls how many latest rounds are used for the small historical averages on the main page. This is separate from the full Statistics window, which can filter by dates and bucket data into raw, 15 minute, one hour, day, week or month views.
help.content.advanced.debug: Debug contains Save debug snapshot after round and Also save full debug history. These should normally stay disabled unless you are investigating a bug or decoder problem. Snapshots are safe for timing because they are written only after a round, not during live Morse, but the history option can create large JSONL files over time.
help.content.advanced.logging: Morsewurst also writes structured JSONL application logs under the active profile data folder, normally in a logs directory. The app log is for local application events and exceptions, while the network log is for network-related events. Log files rotate by size, so they are meant for troubleshooting without filling the profile folder indefinitely.
help.content.network.heading: Morsewurst Network
help.content.network.intro: The Network button opens Morsewurst Network, a WebSocket based prototype for sending live Morse telemetry to other users. It can join public rooms, create or join private rooms and play received Morse locally using a jitter buffer.
help.content.network.callsign: Callsign is the display name shown to other users in the network room. It is saved locally in the active profile network settings. The network also creates a random installation ID and the server stores only a privacy preserving hash of it when the user registry is enabled.
help.content.network.public_rooms: Public rooms are listed by the server and do not require a password. They show the room name, description and user count. The lobby can refresh the room list, request server information and show when public rooms cannot currently be loaded.
help.content.network.private_rooms: Private rooms use a room name and password. They are useful for escaping public noise, but they are not end to end encrypted private conversations. Treat them as simple room separation with password protection. Never send secrets, private information or anything sensitive through a Morsewurst room.
help.content.network.remembered: Remembered private rooms are stored locally on this computer after a successful private room connection. A remembered room can fill the room fields again, and double clicking can join quickly. The server can keep private room metadata such as room key, display name, room ID and password verifier, but not the plain password.
help.content.network.server_info: Server information shows the relay status, public rooms, connected users and similar operational information when the server allows it. The client can also ping the server, which measures round trip time and helps diagnose connection quality.
help.content.network.quality: The jitter buffer makes received Morse smoother by delaying playback slightly and scheduling tones from their original microsecond timestamps. The default buffer is about 750 ms. If packets arrive late, Morsewurst can schedule them immediately, drop very late or stale tones, reset playback after pauses and suggest a higher buffer value.
help.content.network.settings: Network settings include callsign, audio playback, tone frequency, volume, waveform, output device, sample rate, block size, latency, jitter buffer and transmit enabled. Frequency changes the pitch you hear, volume changes local playback loudness and transmit enabled controls whether your own keying is sent to the room.
help.content.network.audio: Network audio settings affect only local received audio. Tone frequency and volume decide how incoming Morse is played on this computer, and playback can be disabled without leaving the room.
help.content.network.radio_noise: Radio channel noise adds local ambience under received Morse. You can choose the noise style, noise tone and noise level. The noise runs only while you are inside a room and is not sent to other users.
help.content.network.noise_ducking: Noise ducking temporarily lowers the radio noise while you transmit and, if enabled, while received tones play. Depth, attack, hold and release control how strongly and how quickly the ambience moves.
help.content.network.transmit: When transmit is enabled, local tone telemetry can be sent to the connected room. When audio playback is enabled, incoming tone messages are played locally. The server relays tone messages to other clients in the room, but it is not designed to store Morse content or raw telemetry history.
help.content.network.note: The public relay is a prototype. The server does not intentionally store Morse content, but it can store limited operational metadata needed for functions such as room persistence, user counts, hashed installation tracking and abuse prevention. Private rooms are automatically removed after the configured idle time, which is one month by default.
help.content.profiles.heading: User profiles
help.content.profiles.intro: Profiles make Morsewurst usable by multiple people on the same computer. Each profile has its own database, settings, debug folder and network settings under the application data directory.
help.content.profiles.create: If no profile exists on first launch, the Create user profile window appears and you must create a profile before using Morsewurst. Later, the User profiles window can add more users.
help.content.profiles.switch: Use profile selects another profile and restarts Morsewurst so the profile specific database and settings can be loaded cleanly. The active profile is shown in the profile list.
help.content.profiles.delete: The active profile cannot be renamed or deleted while it is running, and the last remaining profile cannot be deleted. To rename or delete the current profile, create or choose another temporary profile, restart into it, rename or delete the old profile, then switch back and remove the temporary profile if you no longer need it.
help.content.profiles.language: Language is selected in the Language tab of Settings. Changing the language takes effect after restarting Morsewurst. The help text uses the same i18n system as the rest of the application.
help.content.profiles.storage: Deleting a profile moves the profile folder to a backup location rather than immediately destroying it permanently. Practice session deletion is different. It modifies the active database directly and cannot be undone from the application.
help.content.troubleshooting.heading: Troubleshooting
help.content.troubleshooting.intro: Most problems are caused by serial port conflicts, a wrong input mode, not enough saved history, too strict statistics filters or network timing. The status texts and debug tools are meant to help identify which part is failing.
help.content.troubleshooting.serial: If the serial device does not connect, refresh the port list, check that no other program is using the port and wait if automatic scanning is already running. A compatible Morsewurst device should send the expected heartbeat.
help.content.troubleshooting.keyboard: If Keyboard Morse behaves strangely, remember that computer keyboards are not precision timing devices. Use it for testing and casual practice, but prefer the hardware keyer when timing scores and skill estimates matter.
help.content.troubleshooting.network: If Network rooms do not load, check the server address, internet connection and whether the relay is reachable. Repeated failures are shown in the lobby after consecutive refresh problems. Ping and server info are useful first checks.
help.content.troubleshooting.audio: If received network audio is late or choppy, raise the jitter buffer, use a stable audio output device and avoid very small block sizes unless you know your audio system can handle them. Morsewurst may drop stale tones after sleep, resume or long connection stalls so old buffered sound is not dumped all at once.
help.content.troubleshooting.debug: If you suspect a decoder or scoring bug, enable Save debug snapshot after round. Enable full debug history only when you really need to compare several rounds, because it can grow into a large file. The Debug window can show the latest snapshot, formatted history or raw JSONL, copy visible text, open the debug folder and clear debug data.
help.content.troubleshooting.logs: If the application starts but something behaves unexpectedly, check the profile logs directory. The JSONL logs contain timestamps, event names, messages and sanitized context. They are separate from debug snapshots, which are round-specific decoder and scoring captures.
help.content.troubleshooting.updates: Morsewurst can check for updates from the configured update manifest. Release notes, installer builds and source code are published through the project GitHub repository when available.
help.content.tips.heading: Practical tips
help.content.tips.telemetry: Use real telemetry whenever possible. It gives Morsewurst the data needed to understand what happened, not only what character finally appeared.
help.content.tips.clean_rounds: For useful long term statistics, save clean and honest rounds. Stopping a broken round is better than saving noise as if it were a normal attempt.
help.content.tips.wpm: Raise WPM gradually. A realistic Overall skill WPM is more useful than one unusually fast round, because the skill model rewards repeatable, accurate and understandable Morse.
help.content.tips.problem_chars: Use difficult character practice when you see repeated errors. It works best together with a realistic character mix, because weak letters, weak numbers and weak punctuation are weighted inside their own selected groups.
help.content.tips.character_mix: Use the character mix as a training focus tool. A small punctuation or number share is enough to keep those symbols alive over time, while larger shares are useful when you intentionally want a number-heavy or punctuation-heavy session.
help.content.tips.network: Use Network as a live practice and experimentation space. Public rooms are good for casual testing, while private rooms reduce noise but should not be treated as secure or secret.
help.content.closing: Morsewurst is meant to grow with your practice. The more accurate telemetry and clean saved rounds you give it, the better it can help you understand your Morse rhythm, speed and progress.
